'''Herman, Baron Vanden Berghe''' (Herman van den Berge) (born [[Overboelare]], 12 June 1933, died Oud-Heverlee, 23 January 2017)<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://alamirefoundation.org/nl/organisatie/herman-vanden-berghe |title=Herman Vanden Berghe - Alamire Foundation |access-date=2 January 2014 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304094037/http://alamirefoundation.org/nl/organisatie/herman-vanden-berghe |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://nieuws.kuleuven.be/node/17557 |title=Geneticus Herman Vanden Berghe overleden |language=Dutch |publisher=Katholieke Universiteit Leuven |date=23 January 2017 |accessdate=4 March 2017}}</ref> was a [[Belgians|Belgian]] pioneer in [[human genetics]]. He founded the Centrum voor Menselijke Erfelijkheid ([[Center for Human Genetics]]) at the medical faculty of the [[Katholieke Universiteit Leuven|Catholic University of Leuven]] in [[Leuven]] (Louvain), [[Belgium]]. He was a cytogeneticist and applied [[cytogenetics]] to [[oncology]]. Among other findings, he discovered the deletion 5q syndrome in [[myelodysplasia]]. A native [[Flemish people|Flemish-speaker]], he was also fluent in a number of other languages, including French and English, which facilitated his international role in [[medical genetics]].

Professor Vanden Berghe was granted the title of '''Baron''' by [[Baudouin I]], King of Belgium and from 2000 to 2003 served as chairman of the King Baudouin Foundation. He was a founding member of the International Forum for Biophilosophy established in Belgium by Royal Decree in 1988. The Forum is responsible for the [[Golden Eurydice Award]].
